channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You lose cognitive precision when performing two tasks simultaneously.
item.description: Cognitive load theory shows that your working memory has a limited capacity for information processing.

item.title: Your brain cannot process two independent tasks at once.
item.description: The psychological refractory period causes a delay in reaction to a second stimulus if it arrives during the processing of the first.

item.title: You process sentences faster when they match your physical movement.
item.description: The action-sentence compatibility effect demonstrates that manual reaction times are faster when the sentence describes movement in that direction.

item.title: You recall information best in the same environment you learned it.
item.description: The encoding specificity principle suggests that memory retrieval is aided by cues present during the initial learning event.

item.title: You prioritize trivial tasks because they offer immediate completion.
item.description: The mere urgency effect shows people choose tasks with shorter deadlines over tasks with higher rewards.

item.title: You react faster when your hand matches the stimulus position.
item.description: The Simon effect shows that response times are faster when the stimulus location corresponds to the response location.

item.title: You unconsciously copy the sentence structure of people you speak to.
item.description: Syntactic priming makes you more likely to repeat the grammatical structure of the sentence you just heard.

item.title: Your brain ignores facial details when a face is upside down.
item.description: The Thatcher effect causes inverted faces to appear normal despite grotesque distortions in the eyes and mouth.

item.title: Your attention is wired to follow where others look.
item.description: The gaze cueing effect shows that human attention shifts automatically to follow another person's eyes.

item.title: Your brain actively blocks information you recently chose to ignore.
item.description: Negative priming demonstrates that identifying a target is slower if the item was previously ignored.

item.title: Your brain treats abstract ideas as physical weight.
item.description: Participants holding a heavy clipboard rated job applicants as having more 'serious' and 'significant' personalities.

item.title: You fix mistakes faster when you feel certain.
item.description: Participants were more likely to correct an error if they were 'highly confident' that the wrong answer was actually correct.

item.title: Your environment shapes how you perceive basic lines.
item.description: In a study of 14 societies, people living in 'carpentered' environments were more susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion.

item.title: You link abstract sounds to specific physical shapes.
item.description: Research by Ramachandran and Hubbard (2001) reported that 95% of participants associated the names as described, but this effect is not universal across all cultures.

item.title: Your perception of reality shifts to match others.
item.description: In 1935, Sherif found that people converge on a shared estimate when viewing a stationary dot of light in a dark room.

item.title: You hear sounds differently based on lip movement.
item.description: In a 1976 study, participants reported hearing 'da' when a speaker’s mouth showed 'ga' but the audio played 'ba'.

item.title: You change your opinion to avoid social isolation.
item.description: In a 1951 experiment, 74% of participants went along with an obviously incorrect group judgment at least once.

item.title: You work harder for rewards you did not earn.
item.description: In the 2011 'IKEA Effect' study, participants were willing to pay significantly more—in one experiment, 63% more—for products they assembled themselves compared to those assembled by others.

item.title: You interpret your own physiological arousal incorrectly every day.
item.description: A 1962 study (Schachter and Singer) proposed that physiological arousal is labeled as an emotion (specifically anger or euphoria in their experiments) based on social context.

item.title: You view your past self as a complete stranger.
item.description: A 2009 study found that brain activity patterns when thinking about your future self resemble those for thinking about a different person.

item.title: You consistently overestimate your ability to control external events.
item.description: When an outcome is preceded by your own action, even if it is unrelated, you feel a 'sense of agency' that causes you to believe you caused it.

item.title: You interpret ambiguity based on your current physical comfort.
item.description: Hard chairs make people more 'stubborn' and 'unyielding' during negotiations compared to soft seating.

item.title: You unconsciously adjust your gait to match others.
item.description: When walking with a partner, your stride frequency naturally synchronizes within minutes to match theirs.

item.title: You can misidentify the source of your own thoughts.
item.description: Cryptomnesia occurs when you mistake a forgotten memory for a brand-new, original idea.

item.title: You can temporarily destroy the meaning of any word.
item.description: Semantic satiation is triggered by the high frequency of word repetition over a short period, rather than a specific 30-second threshold.

item.title: You remember more of a scene than you actually saw.
item.description: When you look at an image, your brain 'fills in' the area surrounding the borders.

item.title: You use the same solution for different problems.
item.description: You will stick to an inefficient solution for a problem because it worked on previous ones.

item.title: Your perception of an emotion depends on what came before.
item.description: An identical facial expression is perceived as hunger, grief, or desire depending on the preceding image.

item.title: You are significantly worse at distinguishing faces of other races.
item.description: The 'own-race effect' is a well-documented psychological phenomenon where individuals are more accurate at recognizing faces of their own race compared to other races.

item.title: Comparing two things takes longer when they are similar.
item.description: You identify which of two numbers is larger faster if the distance between them is greater.

item.title: What you wear changes how your brain functions.
item.description: Wearing a garment identified as a doctor's coat reduced the number of errors made on specific selective attention tasks by approximately 50% compared to a control group.

item.title: Your mood determines what you can remember.
item.description: Information is sometimes encoded and retrieved more effectively when the internal emotional state matches between encoding and retrieval, a concept known as mood-dependent memory, though this effect is inconsistent and often difficult to replicate.

item.title: You avoid making choices when you have too much data.
item.description: A 2000 study by Iyengar and Lepper suggested that, in specific conditions, limited choice sets can lead to higher conversion rates than extensive ones.

item.title: You judge people by their actions but yourself by intent.
item.description: Jones and Nisbett (1971) proposed that actors tend to attribute their behavior to situational factors while observers attribute the same behavior to dispositional traits, though this effect has been shown to be weak or inconsistent in later research.

item.title: You overestimate how clearly your feelings show to others.
item.description: In a 1998 study, individuals consistently rated their internal anxiety as being significantly more visible to observers than it actually was.

item.title: You confuse your focus with reality.
item.description: The 'negativity dominance' principle shows that people give disproportionate weight to singular negative features in a multi-attribute evaluation.

item.title: You judge the morality of acts by the outcome.
item.description: Outcome bias makes people judge a decision by its eventual outcome rather than the quality of the decision at the time it was made.

item.title: You are more likely to lie when you feel anonymous.
item.description: Deindividuation reduces the internalized social norms that typically constrain honesty.

item.title: You categorize objects based on how they 'should' work.
item.description: The 'typicality effect' shows that people process category members differently based on how well they fit a prototype.

item.title: You interpret your bodily signals through social context.
item.description: Physiological arousal is ambiguous, and you use your environment to identify what the emotion means.

item.title: You rely on physical warmth to feel social comfort.
item.description: A 2008 study suggested a link between physical and social warmth, though these findings have proven difficult to replicate.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes memories that have high emotional intensity.
item.description: The 'arousal-biased competition' theory explains that arousal enhances memory for high-priority stimuli while impairing memory for low-priority stimuli.

item.title: You overestimate your ability to predict the future.
item.description: The 'hot hand' fallacy leads people to believe that success streaks imply a higher probability of continued success.

item.title: Similar sounding words disrupt your short-term memory.
item.description: Lists of phonologically similar words are significantly harder to memorize than lists of dissimilar-sounding words.

item.title: You perform better when you are slightly stressed.
item.description: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes an inverted-U relationship between stimulus strength and learning performance, originally observed in mice.

item.title: Your brain prefers information that sounds like music.
item.description: Statements that rhyme are judged as more accurate than the same statements written without rhymes.

item.title: Your choices often follow the crowd's momentum.
item.description: The probability of an individual adopting a behavior increases as more people do the same, because individuals use others' actions as signals of information to make more accurate decisions.

item.title: You are less likely to help if others are watching.
item.description: The presence of other witnesses significantly reduces the individual probability that someone will offer help in an emergency.

item.title: You judge a person's character by their appearance.
item.description: The 'halo effect' was identified by Thorndike in 1920, but the specific 'what is beautiful is good' stereotype regarding intelligence and kindness is most famously attributed to a 1972 study.

item.title: You react differently to the same information framed differently.
item.description: The framing effect, where choice is influenced by whether information is presented as gains or losses, was famously explored by Tversky and Kahneman in 1981 using the 'Asian disease' scenario (600 lives) rather than a 90%/10% percentage model.
